photo.title: Anderson Willy with his wife and daughter outside their home in Boseja Ward, Maun. Anderson moved to Maun from the Mbukushu settlement of Etsha in 1982.
The daughter of Anderson Willy sitting outside their home in Boseja Ward, Maun. Anderson moved to Maun from the Mbukushu settlement of Etsha in 1982.
The garden of Anderson Willy and his family, fenced with branches of Mopane wood, in Boseja Ward, Maun. Anderson moved to Maun from the Mbukushu settlement of Etsha in 1982.

A hut and fenced courtyard (lolwapa) in the plot belonging to Jobe Phezo, an Mbukushu woman living in Boseja ward. This hut was previously where her mmangwane (mother's younger sister) lived, but following her death in 1999 is now used for keeping goods and cooking on a fire.

A hut in the plot of Jobe Phezo, a woman living in Boseja ward, showing the preferred Mbukushu method of building, using a meshwork of mopane poles between uprights and packing the gaps with wet soil to dry into place. Many Mbukushu migrants to Maun settled in Boseja ward, on the other side of the Thamalakane River. This hut belonged to the son of one of Jobe's aunts (her cousin).

Huts in the plot of Jobe Phezo, a woman living in Boseja ward, showing the preferred Mbukushu method of building, using a meshwork of mopane poles between uprights and packing the gaps with wet soil to dry into place. Many Mbukushu migrants to Maun settled in Boseja ward, on the other side of the Thamalakane River. The huts shown belong to her brother (white door, closest), the middle one is where she and her female cousin slept, and, further away, the son of one of her aunts (her cousin).

The house of Mombaka Kakuru, an Mbukushu woman living in her brother's plot in Boseja ward. When Mombaka moved to the plot in 1996 it was the rainy season so she built in the typical Mbukushu style, her brother making the structure, a meshwork of dithupa (sticks) and she then went into the bush and collected boloko (fresh dung) which she mixed with mud to fill in between the sticks. She made a lolwapa courtyard fence from the stems of mokodi (wild sage), collected locally.

A house in the plot belonging to the younger brother of Wambe Angere, an Mbukushu woman living in Boseja ward. She was born at Sepupa, where her parents were still living. The hut is made from mopane poles lashed together in a meshwork and plastered in between with soil from termite mounds (mmu wa seolo). The structure for another building can be seen to left.
Matomo James, an Mbukushu man living in Boseja ward, constructing a lolwapa courtyard fence in front of his house using stems of mokodi (wild sage) and lebelebele (millet) from his garden.

House in the plot of Manyema Dibonke, an Mbukushu man living in Boseja ward. He came to Main in 1995 from Nxomoxao near Mohembo, and eventually found this plot with his elder brother in 1997, looking for a better life.
A lidded basket with human form designs incorporated. This basket was displayed in an exhibition at Nhabe Museum, Maun.
A cylindrical basket. This basket was displayed in an exhibition at Nhabe Museum, Maun.
A small plate basket.
A rectilinear hut with grass thatch and walls made from vertical and horizontal wooden staves covered in mud plaster. This style was particularly favoured by Mbukushu migrants in Boseja Ward, Maun.

A hut showing the Mbukushu method of building, using horizontal bands of sticks between uprights and packing the gaps with wet soil to dry into place. The hut facing it uses letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis). Many Mbukushu migrants to Maun settled in Boseja ward, on the other side of the Thamalakane River.

A hut showing the Mbukushu method of building, using horizontal bands of sticks between uprights and packing the gaps with wet soil to dry into place. Many Mbukushu migrants to Maun settled in Boseja ward, on the other side of the Thamalakane River.

A close-up showing the meshwork of mopane poles packed with mud, the preferred Mbukushu method of building in Boseja ward at this time. Many Mbukushu migrants to Maun settled in Boseja ward, on the other side of the Thamalakane River. This hut was in the plot of Jobe Phezo, a woman living in Boseja ward.

A house in the plot belonging to the younger brother of Wambe Angere, an Mbukushu woman living in Boseja ward. The huts show the typical Mbukushu style of building up a meshwork of sticks (dithupa) and packing the spaces with mud to dry in place. Typically, they are then roofed with corrugated tin.
Matomo James, an Mbukushu man living in Boseja ward, constructing a lolwapa courtyard fence in front of his house using stems of mokodi (wild sage) and lebelebele (millet) from his garden.

Two houses in the plot of Manyema Dibonke, an Mbukushu man living in Boseja ward. He came to Main in 1995 from Nxomoxao near Mohembo, and eventually found this plot with his elder brother in 1997, looking for a better life.

Close up view of a lolwapa fence made from the stems of mokodi (wild sage), in the plot of Manyema Dibonke, an Mbukushu man living in Boseja ward. He came to Main in 1995 from Nxomoxao near Mohembo, and eventually found this plot with his elder brother in 1997, looking for a better life.

Hut belonging to the eldest son of Kashiate Mogumbula, an Mbukushu woman living in Boseja ward. She was born in Angola who moved with her parents to Etsha 3, gradually moving to Maun and this ward. She stated that she only found people building like this, using dithupa (a meshwork of sticks) packed with earth, here in Boseja. It seemed to her to be a very localised style in this ward due to difficulties of accessing mud bricks or money for concrete bricks, or money for letlhaka.
A bowl basket. This basket was displayed in an exhibition at Nhabe Museum, Maun.

A plate basket with people, animals, huts and ladders incorporated in the design. This basket was displayed in an exhibition at Nhabe Museum, Maun.

A rectilinear hut with corrugated iron roof and walling made from horizontal and vertical staves plastered with mud, a style favoured by Mbukushu migrants in Maun. In the homestead of Anderson Willy in Boseja Ward. Anderson moved to Maun from the Mbukushu settlement of Etsha in 1982.
Concrete brick house belonging to the brother of Mombaka Kakuru, an Mbukushu woman living in Boseja ward. Mombaka came to live with her brother here in this plot in 1996.

The hut is made from mopane poles lashed together in a meshwork and plastered in between with soil from termite mounds (mmu wa seolo). She has made a lolwapa courtyard fence from mokodi (wild sage) stems.

He came to Main in 1995 from Nxomoxao near Mohembo, and eventually found this plot with his elder brother in 1997, looking for a better life. The house is built using the typical Mbukushu technique found in Boseja at the time, a meshwork of dithupa (sticks) filled in with mmu wa seolo (anthill soil), roofed with corrugated iron.

Hut for visitors, goods, etc., in the plot of Kashiate Mogumbula, an Mbukushu woman living in Boseja ward. She was born in Angola who moved with her parents to Etsha 3, gradually moving to Maun and this ward. She stated that she only found people building like this, using dithupa (a meshwork of sticks) packed with earth, here in Boseja. It seemed to her to be a very localised style in this ward due to difficulties of accessing mud bricks or money for concrete bricks, or money for letlhaka.
The first house built by Kashiate Mogumbula, an Mbukushu woman living in Boseja ward. She was born in Angola who moved with her parents to Etsha 3, gradually moving to Maun and this ward.

Kashiate Mogumbula, an Mbukushu woman living in Boseja ward, sitting outside her lolwapa courtyard. She was born in Angola who moved with her parents to Etsha 3, gradually moving to Maun and this ward. Several of her children have also built houses in the plot, as well as a cousin.

A hut under construction. This shows the technique commonly adopted by Mbukushu migrants in Boseja ward at this time, creating a dense wall of moping poles (dipalalo), which will then be strengthened with horizontally bound sticks (dithupa) to create a meshwork, over which mmu wa seolo (anthill soil) will be plastered. If people could find dung to mix with it, they would, but there were no cattle grazing locally.
